ENT Clinical Note – Video Consultation  

Subjective:  
• Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Progressive reduction in hearing in the LEFT ear for ~6 weeks.  
• Symptom timeline and progression: Onset 6 weeks ago; intermittent. Previously had a 2-day episode of similar hearing difficulty ~1 year ago.  
• ENT symptoms:  
  – Hearing: Unilateral (left) muffled hearing.  
  – Tinnitus: Intermittent ringing in left ear; masking effect when background sound (TV/music) present.  
  – Vestibular: Occasional mild off-balance sensation; no true spinning vertigo; no associated nausea.  
  – No ear pain, otorrhea, pruritus, or itching.  
  – No throat tightness, dysphagia, dyspnea, nasal/ocular symptoms, facial/tongue swelling, voice change, stridor, or neck/ear fullness reported.  
• Relevant past episodes and treatments: Brief (2-day) unilateral hearing difficulty 1 year ago; resolved spontaneously. No prior otologic procedures or treatment.  
• Allergies: Not documented.  
• Current medications: Not documented.  
• Social context: Patient alone but in a private setting during video call.

Objective:  
• Observable swelling: None reported.  
• Airway/breathing: No distress; normal speech noted via video.  
• Mental status: Alert and oriented; no syncope or dizziness at time of call.  
• Vitals / physical examination: Not recorded (video visit; no otoscopy performed).  
• Presence of caregiver/companion: None.

Assessment:  
Working impression: Unilateral reduced hearing with tinnitus – highest suspicion for conductive cause such as cerumen impaction; alternative inner-/middle-ear causes to be ruled out.  

Evidence summary: Gradual, unilateral loss with intermittent tinnitus; no pain or discharge; age 32.  

DDx (aligned with transcript and DDx list):  
1. Cerumen impaction – most common reversible cause; consistent with gradual unilateral loss and tinnitus; clinician plan to rule out.  
2. Menière’s disease – fits loss + tinnitus + mild disequilibrium, though vertigo absent and symptom pattern atypical.  
3. Serous otitis media / Eustachian-tube dysfunction – possible conductive loss; no URI symptoms (opposing evidence).  

Plan:  
• Arrange face-to-face GP/ENT clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopic examination to assess for wax impaction, middle-ear effusion, or other pathology.  
• Provide patient with tinnitus information leaflet; advise reading before in-person review.  
• If cerumen impaction confirmed, proceed with removal (microsuction/irrigation per clinic protocol).  
• Escalation instructions: Seek urgent review if sudden complete hearing loss, onset of true vertigo, severe dizziness, ear pain/discharge, facial weakness, or new neurological symptoms.  
• Contact details: Patient to phone support team (number provided in consultation notes) to book appointment; may book repeat video consultation if interim issues arise.  
• Follow-up: Reassess after otoscopy; consider audiometry and ENT referral if hearing loss persists or if sensorineural pathology suspected.

Quality checks (document_quality):  
● Missing expected elements: Detailed allergy list, current medication list (dose/route/frequency), occupational/noise exposure history, family otologic history, vitals, formal audiometry.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None significant noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional minor pauses but clinically adequate.
